etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French extreme, from Latin extrēmus, the superlative of exter.

definitions.definition: Of a place, the most remote, farthest or outermost.
In the greatest or highest degree; intense.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XIII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: And Vickers launched forth into a tirade very different from his platform utterances. He spoke with extreme contempt of the dense stupidity exhibited on all occasions by the working classes. He said that if you wanted to do anything for them, you must rule them, not pamper them.

definitions.definition: Excessive, or far beyond the norm.

quote.citation: 2013 March, Frank Fish, George Lauder, “Not Just Going with the Flow”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 2, page 114:
quote.text: An extreme version of vorticity is a vortex. The vortex is a spinning, cyclonic mass of fluid, which can be observed in the rotation of water going down a drain, as well as in smoke rings, tornados and hurricanes.

definitions.definition: Of sports, difficult or dangerous; performed in a hazardous environment.
The greatest or utmost point, degree, or condition.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter II, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Sunning himself on the board steps, I saw for the first time Mr. Farquhar Fenelon Cooke. […] A silver snaffle on a heavy leather watch guard which connected the pockets of his corduroy waistcoat, together with a huge gold stirrup in his Ascot tie, sufficiently proclaimed his tastes. […] But withal there was a perceptible acumen about the man which was puzzling in the extreme.

definitions.definition: Each of the things at opposite ends of a range or scale.

quote.citation: 2017, Anthony J. McMichael, Alistair Woodward, Cameron Muir, Climate Change and the Health of Nations, →ISBN, page 56:
quote.text: Most public discussion about heat extremes refers to risks faced by the general community. Yet even greater extremes of heat exposure do and will occur in many occupational settings, posing special risks to health, behavior, and work capacity.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, plural only) One of the last moments of life.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act III, scene ii:
quote.text: a farther paſſion feeds my thoughts,With ceaſeleſſe and diſconſolate conceits,Which dies my lookes so liueleſſe as they are,And might, if my extreames had ful euents,Make me the gaſtly counterfeit of death.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) Either of the two numbers at the ends of a proportion, as 1 and 6 in 1:2=3:6.

quote.citation: 1796, Charles Burney, Memoirs of the Life and Writings of Metastasio, section 2.5:
quote.text: In the empty and extreme cold theatre.
